title: US labor-market power cannot be read from wage markdowns alone
source_unit: US labor-market-power literature, firm-specific residual labor-supply elasticity, search frictions, worker preferences, employer concentration, and wage-setting practices
geography: United States and comparative labor-market evidence reviewed for US policy analysis

observations.period: Working paper issued August 2026; review of recent labor-market-power evidence

denominator.unit: review article and cited empirical literature; no single population denominator

labor_power_definition.unit: firm-specific residual labor-supply elasticity is the organizing definition of labor-market power

power_sources.unit: search frictions, preference heterogeneity, and employer concentration are distinct sources that can be nested in the framework

markdown_elasticity_non_equivalence.unit: wage markdowns and labor-supply elasticities cannot be inferred from one another without accounting for wage-setting practices

policy_scope.unit: antitrust, labor regulation, immigration, and macroeconomic policy can interact with monopsony

observations.method: Review and synthesis of labor-market-power theory and empirical estimates, with a framework illustrating how monopsony interacts with efficiency wages and firm wage-setting.
observations.uncertainty: This is a review/framework paper, not a new population estimate or causal policy evaluation. It does not identify one US industry's power, establish a worker welfare effect, or provide a single preferred elasticity for all firms.
observations.subgroup: Workers and firms whose observed wages, outside options, search conditions, preferences, concentration exposure, and wage-setting practices differ.
observations.counterinterpretation: A low observed markdown may reflect high labor-supply elasticity or efficient wage-setting rather than weak firm power; a low elasticity may reflect worker preferences or search costs rather than employer concentration alone.

related_sources.claim: Worker heterogeneity explains much of the modeled variation in labor-supply elasticities and wage markdowns.
US product-market rivalry and cost-of-capital shocks shape firm investment, markups, and concentration.
US overtime coverage changed earnings and employer classification responses without a detected employment decline.

boundary: This record supplies a measurement framework for the US firm-power chain. It does not substitute for industry-level worker, firm, customer, or household outcome evidence and should not be used to rank firms by power without compatible elasticity, wage-setting, outside-option, and concentration measures.
